theory.title: The chain rule behind learning
theory.prompt: Let prediction = 3w + 1 and L = (prediction - 7)². At w=1, give the derivative and the updated weight after one gradient-descent step with learning rate 0.1.
theory.concepts: A derivative measures local sensitivity: how much a small change in an input changes an output. For a composition L(g(w)), the chain rule multiplies the outer sensitivity dL/dg by the inner sensitivity dg/dw. Backpropagation applies this rule through a computation graph. Gradient descent moves opposite the gradient, since the gradient points toward the steepest local increase. A finite step is only a local approximation and can overshoot if its learning rate is too large.
hints: Differentiate the square first, then the linear prediction.
At w=1 the prediction is below the target.
steps: Write r = 3w+1-7 = 3w-6, so L=r².
Apply the chain rule: dL/dw = 2r × 3 = 6(3w-6).
At w=1, r=-3 and the derivative is -18.
Update w_new = 1 - 0.1(-18) = 2.8. A negative gradient increases w. Here the loss drops from 9 to 5.76, although the optimum w=2 is overshot.
rubric: Derivative is -18.
Updated weight is 2.8.
Explains chain rule and negative-gradient direction.
theory.discussionPrompt: Let prediction = 3w + 1 and loss L = (prediction - 7)². Find dL/dw at w=1, then take one gradient descent step with learning rate 0.1. Explain the sign of the update.

theory.title: From partial derivatives to a gradient
theory.prompt: For f(x,y)=x²+3xy+2y², compute the gradient at (1,2). Give a unit direction of steepest increase and explain what a partial derivative holds fixed.
theory.concepts: A partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the others constant. The gradient stacks these partial derivatives into a vector. For a unit direction u, the directional derivative is gradient(f)·u. Cauchy–Schwarz shows this is largest when u points along the gradient. The gradient depends on the point and on the coordinate scaling; feature normalization can therefore change the behavior of optimization.
hints: Differentiate once with respect to x and once with respect to y.
Normalize the resulting vector by its Euclidean length.
steps: ∂f/∂x = 2x+3y and ∂f/∂y = 3x+4y.
At (1,2), gradient(f) = (8,11).
The length is sqrt(8²+11²)=sqrt(185).
The steepest-increase unit direction is (8,11)/sqrt(185); its negative is steepest descent.
rubric: Both partial derivatives are correct.
Gradient is (8,11).
Unit direction is normalized and other coordinates are held fixed.

theory.title: A local linear approximation
theory.prompt: Use a first-order Taylor approximation of log(x) around x=1 to estimate log(1.05). Enter the approximation only.
theory.concepts: First-order Taylor expansion approximates f(a+h) by f(a)+f′(a)h. It replaces a smooth function by its tangent line near a. The neglected leading term is approximately ½f″(a)h², so reducing the step often reduces error quadratically. For concave functions such as log, the tangent lies above the graph. This same local approximation explains the gradient-based direction chosen in optimization.
hints: log(1)=0 and the derivative of log(x) is 1/x.
The second derivative is negative.
steps: Choose a=1 and h=0.05.
Compute f(a)=0 and f′(a)=1.
Approximate log(1.05) by 0+1×0.05=0.05.
Since f″(x)=-1/x²<0, the tangent overestimates. The actual value is about 0.04879; the approximation loses accuracy farther from 1.
rubric: Approximation is 0.05.
Explains the tangent-line formula.
Identifies overestimation using concavity.
theory.discussionPrompt: Use a first-order Taylor approximation of log(x) around x=1 to estimate log(1.05). Explain why the approximation is local and whether it overestimates the true value.

theory.title: Stationary point or minimum?
theory.prompt: Compare stationary points of f(x)=x² and g(x)=x³. Is a zero derivative enough to prove a minimum? How does convexity help?
theory.concepts: A stationary point has zero first derivative, which is a necessary condition for an unconstrained interior differentiable minimum, but not sufficient. The second derivative describes local curvature. Strictly positive second derivative at a stationary point gives a strict local minimum. A differentiable convex function lies above each tangent line, so any stationary point is a global minimum. Neural-network losses are generally nonconvex, so the same global guarantee does not apply.
hints: Both derivatives vanish at zero.
Check signs or curvature around zero.
steps: For f, f′=2x vanishes at zero and f″=2>0, so zero is a strict minimum.
For g, g′=3x² vanishes at zero, but g takes negative and positive values on either side.
Zero is a stationary inflection point of g, not a minimum.
A zero derivative alone is insufficient. Convexity would guarantee that any stationary point is globally minimizing.
rubric: Distinguishes the two stationary points.
Does not claim zero gradient proves a minimum.
States the convex global-minimum guarantee.

theory.title: Optimization with a constraint
theory.prompt: Minimize x²+y² subject to x+y=6 using a Lagrange multiplier. Explain geometrically why the solution is balanced.
theory.concepts: A constrained optimum cannot usually be found by setting the unconstrained gradient to zero. For an equality constraint h=0 with nonzero constraint gradient, a regular constrained optimum has objective gradient parallel to the constraint gradient. The Lagrangian incorporates this using a multiplier. This gives candidate points, not automatically proof of a global optimum; convexity or direct reasoning supplies that proof here.
hints: Use L=x²+y²+λ(x+y-6).
The stationarity equations imply x=y.
steps: Set 2x+λ=0, 2y+λ=0, and x+y-6=0.
Subtract the first two equations to get x=y.
The constraint gives x=y=3, λ=-6, and objective 18.
The line x+y=6 is closest to the origin at (3,3). The objective is strictly convex and the feasible set is affine, proving this is the unique minimum.
rubric: Correct stationarity equations.
Solution (3,3) and objective 18.
Explains why the candidate is globally optimal.

theory.title: Reason about matrix shapes
theory.prompt: A batch X has shape (32,10), weights W have shape (10,4), and bias b has shape (4,). What is the shape of XW+b? Describe one output element and explain why reversing X and W fails.
theory.concepts: Matrix multiplication contracts matching inner dimensions: (n,d) @ (d,k) produces (n,k). Each output is a dot product between one input row and one weight column. Bias broadcasting adds a shared output offset across examples. Shape reasoning often catches ML bugs before numerical testing. Elementwise multiplication is a different operation and generally cannot replace a matrix product.
hints: Match the inner dimensions.
The bias has one value per output feature.
steps: The contracted dimension is 10, leaving (32,4).
Output[i,j] = sum over k of X[i,k]W[k,j] + b[j].
The bias broadcasts from (4,) to each of the 32 rows.
W @ X would require 4=32, which is false. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.
rubric: Output shape (32,4).
Correct dot-product interpretation.
Explains broadcasting and invalid reversed dimensions.

theory.title: Projection and least squares
theory.prompt: For X=[[1],[2]] and y=[1,3], find the least-squares scalar weight with no intercept. Enter the weight only.
theory.concepts: Least squares minimizes ||y-Xw||². Differentiating gives the normal equations XᵀXw=Xᵀy. With full column rank, the solution is unique. Predictions are the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X; the residual is perpendicular to every column. In numerical code, a QR or SVD-based least-squares solver is preferable to explicitly forming an inverse, especially for nearly dependent features.
hints: Compute XᵀX and Xᵀy.
Check Xᵀ(y-Xw).
steps: Solve 5w=7 to get w=1.4.
Predictions are [1.4,2.8], giving residual y-prediction=[-0.4,0.2].
Xᵀ residual = -0.4+2(0.2)=0. The errors cannot be reduced by moving within the available one-dimensional prediction space.
rubric: Weight 1.4.
Correct predictions and residual.
Verifies orthogonality and explains projection.
theory.discussionPrompt: For X=[[1],[2]] and y=[1,3], find the least-squares scalar weight with no intercept. Compute predictions and show that the residual is orthogonal to the column of X.

theory.title: Eigenvectors and principal directions
theory.prompt: A centered dataset has covariance [[4,0],[0,1]]. What fraction of total variance does its first principal component explain?
theory.concepts: An eigenvector v satisfies Av=λv: the linear map changes its scale but not its direction. A symmetric covariance matrix has orthogonal eigenvectors and nonnegative eigenvalues. PCA chooses directions with maximum projected variance, so the leading eigenvector corresponds to the largest eigenvalue. Centering is essential. Scaling features changes the covariance and can change which direction PCA selects; explained variance does not imply predictive importance for a target.
hints: For a diagonal matrix, the diagonal entries are eigenvalues.
Divide the leading eigenvalue by the sum.
steps: The coordinate directions [1,0] and [0,1] are eigenvectors with eigenvalues 4 and 1.
The first principal component is [1,0], up to sign.
Total variance is the trace, 4+1=5.
The first component explains 4/5=80% of the variance. It ignores labels and need not be the most predictive feature.
rubric: Eigenvalues 4 and 1.
First direction is the first coordinate, up to sign.
Explained variance is 80%.
theory.discussionPrompt: A centered dataset has covariance matrix [[4,0],[0,1]]. Give its eigenvalues and the first principal component direction. What fraction of variance does that component explain?

theory.title: Curvature from a Hessian
theory.prompt: For f(w)=½wᵀAw with A=[[2,0],[0,6]], give the gradient, Hessian, and minimizer. Why is the minimum unique?
theory.concepts: For symmetric A, a quadratic ½wᵀAw has gradient Aw and Hessian A. A positive definite matrix satisfies vᵀAv>0 for every nonzero v, equivalently all eigenvalues are positive for symmetric matrices. Positive definite curvature means strict convexity and a unique stationary minimum. A positive semidefinite matrix may have flat directions and multiple minimizers.
hints: Differentiate each coordinate of w₁²+3w₂².
Check the two diagonal eigenvalues.
steps: Expand f=w₁²+3w₂².
Gradient is (2w₁,6w₂)=Aw, and Hessian is A.
Set the gradient to zero to obtain w=(0,0).
Both eigenvalues, 2 and 6, are positive, so f is strictly convex and the minimum is unique.
rubric: Correct gradient and Hessian.
Minimizer is the zero vector.
Connects positive eigenvalues to uniqueness.

theory.title: Correlated features and unstable weights
theory.prompt: Two regression features are almost identical. Why can coefficients become unstable even if predictions look reasonable? Suggest two remedies.
theory.concepts: Nearly dependent columns make the design matrix poorly conditioned. Different large coefficient combinations can cancel and produce almost the same prediction, so small data perturbations can cause large coefficient changes. This makes individual coefficient interpretation fragile. Ridge adds a positive penalty to coefficient magnitude, stabilizing the fitted system. Removing redundant features or using an SVD-based solver can also help, although numerical solvers alone do not eliminate statistical non-identifiability.
hints: Imagine increasing one coefficient while decreasing the other.
Separate numerical stability from the modeling choice.
steps: With x₁≈x₂, the prediction β₁x₁+β₂x₂ depends mostly on β₁+β₂.
Many coefficient pairs give nearly equal predictions; noise can change which pair is fitted.
Use ridge regularization or remove/combine a redundant feature; standardize before applying comparable penalties.
Use a robust QR/SVD solver, inspect conditioning, and avoid interpreting the two coefficients independently.
rubric: Explains cancellation and instability.
Gives two valid remedies.
Distinguishes stable prediction from reliable coefficient interpretation.

theory.title: Bayes and rare-event detection
theory.prompt: A condition affects 2% of people. A test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Given a positive result, what is the probability of the condition? Enter a fraction, decimal, or percentage.
theory.concepts: Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional probability: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Sensitivity is P(positive|condition); specificity is P(negative|no condition). The positive predictive value depends strongly on prevalence. A test can have high sensitivity and specificity while most positive results are false positives when the condition is rare. Assume a representative person and that the stated rates apply to this population.
hints: Use a hypothetical population of 10,000.
Count true positives and false positives separately.
steps: Among 10,000 people, 200 have the condition and 9,800 do not.
Expected true positives: 0.90×200=180. Expected false positives: 0.05×9,800=490.
All positives total 670, so P(condition|positive)=180/670≈0.2687.
The answer is about 26.9%, not 90%. This uses the given prevalence and population-specific test rates.
rubric: Uses both true and false positives.
Posterior is about 26.9%.
Distinguishes sensitivity from the posterior.
theory.discussionPrompt: A condition affects 2% of people. A test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. If a person tests positive, what is the probability they have the condition? State the assumptions.

theory.title: Disjoint does not mean independent
theory.prompt: Roll a fair six-sided die. A is “even” and B is “greater than 4.” Are A and B independent? Then explain why two disjoint events with positive probability cannot be independent.
theory.concepts: Events are independent when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), or equivalently learning one does not change the probability of the other when the conditional is defined. Disjoint events cannot both occur, so their intersection has probability zero. This is different from independence. Independence is a property of the joint distribution, not merely of different event labels.
hints: List A, B, and their intersection.
Compare intersection probability with the product.
steps: A∩B={6}, with probability 1/6, equal to (1/2)(1/3). They are independent.
For disjoint events, P(A∩B)=0.
If both marginal probabilities are positive, P(A)P(B)>0, so the independence equality fails.
rubric: Correctly concludes independence for the die example.
Checks the intersection criterion.
Explains why positive-probability disjoint events are dependent.

theory.title: Sampling without replacement
theory.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue tokens. Draw 3 without replacement. What is the probability of exactly 2 red tokens?
theory.concepts: Combinations count unordered subsets: choose(n,k)=n!/[k!(n-k)!]. Sampling without replacement changes the color probability after each draw, so draws are dependent. A hypergeometric count uses combinations of successful and unsuccessful items divided by all equally likely subsets. The binomial model instead assumes a fixed success probability across independent trials.
hints: Choose 2 of the 4 red and 1 of the 6 blue.
Divide by all ways to choose 3 of 10.
steps: There are choose(10,3)=120 equally likely three-token subsets.
Favorable subsets: choose(4,2)×choose(6,1)=6×6=36.
Probability is 36/120=0.3.
A binomial model with p=0.4 assumes replacement or independent fixed-probability draws; that assumption fails here.
rubric: Uses combinations correctly.
Probability is 0.3.
Explains dependence without replacement.
theory.discussionPrompt: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue tokens. Draw 3 without replacement. Find the probability of exactly 2 red tokens. Explain why a binomial model is not exact.

theory.title: The birthday collision approximation
theory.prompt: Give the exact expression for the probability of at least one shared birthday among 30 people. Then approximate it. Assume independent uniform birthdays over 365 days.
theory.concepts: Collision probabilities are easier to calculate using the complement: no collision. As each person joins, fewer birthdays remain unused. For modest group sizes, log(1-x)≈-x leads to the approximation P(no collision)≈exp(-n(n-1)/(2m)) for m equally likely categories. The independence and uniformity assumptions idealize real birthdays; the same structure appears in hashing.
hints: Multiply the successive probabilities of avoiding all previous birthdays.
Approximate the product using the sum of 0 through 29.
steps: P(no match)=product from k=0 to 29 of (365-k)/365.
Thus P(at least one)=1 minus that product.
Approximate the product as exp(-30×29/(2×365))=exp(-1.19178).
The approximation is about 0.6963; the exact value is about 0.7063. Pair collisions are not mutually independent, so simply summing pair probabilities is not exact.
rubric: Uses the complement product.
Approximation is around 70%.
States assumptions and avoids treating pair collisions as independent.

theory.title: Expectation without independence
theory.prompt: A fair die is rolled 12 times. What is the expected number of rolls showing 6?
theory.concepts: An indicator I is one when an event happens and zero otherwise, with E[I]=P(event). Counts are sums of indicators. Expectation is linear even when variables are dependent: E[sum I_i]=sum E[I_i]. Independence matters for simplifying variance and for identifying a binomial distribution, but not for this expectation identity.
hints: Represent each roll’s success by a zero-one indicator.
Sum 12 marginal success probabilities.
steps: Define I_i=1 if roll i is 6, otherwise 0.
N=I₁+…+I₁₂.
Linearity does not require independence. Independent rolls additionally make N binomial, but that is not needed to compute its mean.
rubric: Expected count is 2.
Defines indicators.
Correctly states independence is unnecessary for linearity.
theory.discussionPrompt: A fair die is rolled 12 times. Let N count the rolls showing 6. Find E[N]. Explain the indicator method and whether independence is required for linearity of expectation.

theory.title: Variance of a sum
theory.prompt: X and Y have variances 4 and 9, and covariance -2. Find Var(X+Y) and Corr(X,Y).
theory.concepts: Variance measures spread around a mean. Covariance measures linear co-movement, with units from both variables. Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Correlation divides covariance by the standard deviations and lies between -1 and 1 when both variances are positive. Zero correlation generally does not imply independence; nonlinear dependence can remain.
hints: The standard deviations are 2 and 3.
Do not omit the factor of two on covariance.
steps: If covariance is zero, the variance of the sum is 13 and correlation is zero.
Zero covariance alone does not prove independence. For example X and X² can be uncorrelated under a symmetric distribution while dependent.
rubric: Variance is 9.
Correlation is -1/3.
Does not confuse zero covariance with independence.
theory.discussionPrompt: X and Y have variances 4 and 9, and covariance -2. Find Var(X+Y) and Corr(X,Y). What changes if the covariance is zero?

theory.title: Condition on a useful first step
theory.prompt: A fair coin selects machine A or B. Their defect probabilities are 0.1 and 0.3. Give the overall defect probability and the probability an item came from B given it is defective.
theory.concepts: The law of total probability partitions an event across mutually exclusive, exhaustive cases. P(D)=sum_m P(D|m)P(m). Bayes then reverses the conditioning. Conditioning is often the easiest way to solve an interview problem: choose a state or first action that makes the remaining calculation simple. A mixture’s aggregate rate can hide substantial differences across its components.
hints: Average the two rates with selection weights 1/2.
For the posterior, divide the B-and-defect probability by all defects.
steps: Although the machines are equally likely before inspection, a defect shifts probability toward B because B produces defects more often.
rubric: Overall defect probability 0.2.
Posterior for B is 0.75.
Shows total probability before Bayes.
theory.discussionPrompt: A fair coin selects a machine. Machine A produces a defect with probability 0.1; machine B with probability 0.3. Find the overall defect probability and the probability that a defective item came from B.

theory.title: Choose a probability distribution
theory.prompt: Name reasonable distributions for: successes in 20 independent p=0.2 trials; number of arrivals in an hour at constant rate 3; waiting time to the next arrival; and trials until the first Bernoulli success. Give each expectation and assumptions.
theory.concepts: Distribution choice encodes assumptions. Binomial counts a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials. A homogeneous Poisson process has independent stationary increments; its interval counts are Poisson and waiting times exponential. A geometric distribution models independent discrete trials until success. Parameterization matters: geometric may count either failures or total trials, so always state the convention.
hints: Distinguish a count in a fixed interval from a waiting time.
Use geometric on {1,2,…} for total trials.
steps: Success count is Binomial(n=20,p=0.2), with expectation np=4.
Hour arrivals are Poisson(λ=3), mean 3, under the homogeneous Poisson-process assumptions.
Waiting time is Exponential(rate=3 per hour), mean 1/3 hour.
Trials until first success are Geometric(p=0.2) on {1,2,…}, mean 1/p=5. Rates must use consistent time units.
rubric: Names all four distributions.
Gives means 4, 3, 1/3 hour, and 5.
States independence/rate assumptions and geometric convention.

theory.title: What the central limit theorem says
theory.prompt: IID measurements have mean 10 and standard deviation 4. Using a normal approximation, what is the probability that the mean of 64 observations exceeds 11? Give a decimal or percentage.
theory.concepts: The central limit theorem concerns a normalized sum or mean, not the shape of the original population. With iid observations and finite positive variance, the mean becomes approximately normal as sample size grows. Its standard deviation, the standard error, is σ/sqrt(n). The adequacy of a finite-sample approximation depends on skewness and tails; n=30 or any other fixed threshold is not a universal guarantee.
hints: The sample mean has standard error 4/sqrt(64).
Convert 11 to a standard normal z-score.
steps: E[mean]=10 and SE=4/8=0.5.
Standardize: z=(11-10)/0.5=2.
Using a normal approximation, P(mean>11)≈P(Z>2)≈0.0228.
The CLT approximates the sampling distribution of the mean. The underlying measurements may be non-normal, provided the stated conditions and a reasonable approximation hold.
rubric: Standard error 0.5.
Probability approximately 2.28%.
Distinguishes the mean distribution from raw data.
theory.discussionPrompt: Independent identically distributed measurements have mean 10 and standard deviation 4. Approximate the probability that the mean of 64 observations exceeds 11. Explain why the raw observations need not be normal.

theory.title: The maximum of uniform samples
theory.prompt: X₁,…,Xₙ are independent Uniform(0,1). Derive the CDF of their maximum M and its expected value.
theory.concepts: A cumulative distribution function is F(t)=P(X≤t). A maximum is at most t exactly when every sample is at most t. Independence converts the joint probability into a product. Differentiating a continuous CDF gives its density; expectation is then the integral of x times that density. Order statistics appear in extreme-value reasoning and selection effects.
hints: Write the event M≤t in terms of every X_i.
Differentiate tⁿ, then integrate t times the density.
steps: For 0≤t≤1, P(M≤t)=P(X₁≤t,…,Xₙ≤t)=tⁿ.
The full CDF is 0 below 0, tⁿ on [0,1], and 1 above 1.
The density on (0,1) is nt^(n-1).
E[M]=integral from 0 to 1 of ntⁿ dt=n/(n+1). As n grows, the maximum approaches 1.
rubric: Derives the product using independence.
Gives a valid piecewise CDF.
Expectation n/(n+1).

theory.title: A two-state Markov chain
theory.prompt: From A, a system stays in A with probability 0.8. From B, it moves to A with probability 0.3. Give the stationary probabilities of A and B.
theory.concepts: A Markov chain assumes the next-state distribution depends on the current state rather than the entire history. A row-stochastic transition matrix contains nonnegative rows summing to one. A stationary row distribution π satisfies πP=π and sums to one. Stationarity is an invariant distribution; convergence from arbitrary starting states additionally requires conditions such as irreducibility and aperiodicity in a finite chain.
hints: Use row and column order A,B.
Solve π_A=0.8π_A+0.3π_B.
steps: P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]]. Each row sums to one.
Let π=[a,1-a]. The A balance equation is a=0.8a+0.3(1-a).
Rearrange: 0.5a=0.3, so a=0.6 and π_B=0.4.
Both states communicate and have self-loops, so this finite chain also converges to [0.6,0.4].
rubric: Correct transition matrix convention.
Stationary distribution (0.6,0.4).
Distinguishes stationarity from generic convergence.
theory.discussionPrompt: A system is in states A or B. From A it stays in A with probability 0.8. From B it moves to A with probability 0.3. Write the transition matrix and find the stationary distribution.

theory.title: A fair random walk
theory.prompt: A walk starts at zero and takes 100 independent +1/-1 steps with equal probability. Give its expected final position and variance.
theory.concepts: A random walk is a cumulative sum of increments. For independent mean-zero ±1 increments, means add to zero and variances add to the number of steps. Typical displacement scales as sqrt(n), despite zero average signed displacement. A martingale has conditional expected future value equal to the current value under an appropriate information filtration; this fair walk is an example.
hints: Each increment has mean zero and variance one.
A zero mean does not imply zero spread.
steps: For one step Z, E[Z]=0 and Var(Z)=E[Z²]=1.
For S₁₀₀=sum Z_i, E[S₁₀₀]=0.
Independence gives Var(S₁₀₀)=100 and standard deviation 10.
Signed positions cancel in the mean. Individual walks can be far from zero; zero mean does not mean small absolute displacement.
rubric: Mean 0 and variance 100.
Uses independence for variance.
Explains spread despite zero mean.
theory.discussionPrompt: A walk starts at zero and makes 100 independent steps, each +1 or -1 with equal probability. Find its expected final position and variance. Is its distance from zero always small because the mean is zero?

theory.title: Brownian motion intuition
theory.prompt: For standard Brownian motion W, give the distribution of W(5)-W(2), its variance, and its relationship with W(2). Why is an ordinary smooth derivative an inappropriate model for a Brownian path?
theory.concepts: Standard Brownian motion starts at zero, has continuous paths, and has independent Gaussian increments: an increment over duration Δt has mean zero and variance Δt. Its typical size scales as sqrt(Δt), not Δt. Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable, so stochastic calculus cannot simply treat dW as an ordinary velocity times dt. This is an intuition topic here; solving stochastic differential equations is optional for introductory ML interviews.
hints: Only the time difference matters for an increment’s variance.
Brownian increments are independent of the past.
steps: The elapsed time is 5-2=3.
W(5)-W(2) is Normal(mean=0,variance=3), with standard deviation sqrt(3).
It is independent of W(2), since it is an increment after time 2.
Dividing a typical sqrt(Δt) increment by Δt gives scale 1/sqrt(Δt), which does not behave like a finite smooth velocity as Δt shrinks.
rubric: Normal(0,3), with 3 identified as variance.
Independence from W(2).
Explains rough paths and sqrt-time scaling.

theory.title: Dynamic programming from a recurrence
theory.prompt: You may climb 1 or 2 stairs per move. How many distinct ordered sequences of moves reach stair 5?
theory.concepts: Dynamic programming applies when subproblems overlap and larger answers can be assembled from smaller ones. A recurrence must partition solutions without double-counting. Here the final move is either one stair or two, so the preceding state uniquely identifies a smaller problem. Memoization caches recursive results; tabulation computes them bottom-up. Counting sequences is different from counting unordered combinations.
hints: Partition sequences by their final step.
There is one way to reach stair zero: take no steps.
steps: Let ways(n) count sequences. Set ways(0)=1 and ways(1)=1.
For n≥2, ways(n)=ways(n-1)+ways(n-2).
Values are 1,1,2,3,5,8 for n=0,…,5; the answer is 8.
Keep only the preceding two counts for O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary storage under fixed-width arithmetic. Python integer size grows with n.
rubric: Valid recurrence and base cases.
Answer 8.
Explains overlapping subproblems and iterative complexity.
theory.discussionPrompt: You may climb 1 or 2 stairs at a time. How many distinct sequences reach stair 5? Derive a recurrence, define base cases, and give time and space costs of an iterative solution.

theory.title: Estimate an integral by simulation
theory.prompt: Let U be Uniform(0,1). Use Monte Carlo to estimate the integral of x² from 0 to 1. Give an unbiased estimator, its exact expectation, and how its standard error changes if you use 100 times as many samples.
theory.concepts: Integration over a uniform domain can be written as an expectation. The sample mean of independent function evaluations estimates that expectation without needing a symbolic antiderivative. For finite variance, its standard error falls as 1/sqrt(n), a slow rate independent of dimension in the basic variance formula. A random seed supports reproducibility but is not a substitute for uncertainty estimates.
hints: Average squared independent uniform samples.
Standard error scales as the reciprocal square root of sample count.
steps: Draw iid U₁,…,Uₙ from Uniform(0,1). Use estimate=(1/n)sum U_i².
E[estimate]=E[U²]=integral x² dx=1/3, so it is unbiased.
SE=sqrt(4/(45n)). Multiplying n by 100 divides SE by 10, not 100.
rubric: Unbiased sample-mean estimator.
Expectation 1/3.
Standard error decreases by a factor of 10.

theory.title: Check a gradient numerically
theory.prompt: For f(x)=x³ at x=2, compute the central difference [f(x+h)-f(x-h)]/(2h) with h=0.01.
theory.concepts: Central differences approximate f′(x) using [f(x+h)-f(x-h)]/(2h). For sufficiently smooth f, the leading truncation error is O(h²). Floating-point subtraction of almost equal values loses relative precision; division by a tiny h amplifies that error. Gradient checks therefore balance truncation and rounding error. Use deterministic functions and double precision when diagnosing an implementation.
hints: The exact derivative is 3x².
Expand (x+h)³-(x-h)³.
steps: For a cubic the expression simplifies to 3x²+h².
At x=2 and h=0.01 it equals 12.0001, compared with exact derivative 12.
Shrinking h initially helps, but eventually cancellation and rounding dominate. Compare relative and absolute errors rather than demanding exact equality.
rubric: Correct central difference.
Approximation 12.0001 and exact 12.
Explains truncation versus rounding.
theory.discussionPrompt: Describe a central finite-difference check for the derivative of f(x)=x³ at x=2. Compute it with h=0.01 and explain why an extremely tiny h can make the check worse.

theory.title: Newton versus gradient descent
theory.prompt: For f(w)=(w-3)², start at w=0. Give the result of one gradient-descent step with learning rate 0.1, and of one Newton minimization step.
theory.concepts: Gradient descent uses the slope and a chosen learning rate. Newton minimization also uses curvature: in one dimension, w_new=w-f′(w)/f″(w). In multiple dimensions it solves a Hessian linear system rather than simply dividing. For an exact positive-definite quadratic, Newton can reach the minimizer in one step. Hessians are costly for high-dimensional networks, and indefinite or near-singular curvature requires damping or other safeguards.
hints: Apply the two update formulas separately.
steps: At w=0, gradient=-6 and Hessian=2.
Gradient descent gives 0-0.1(-6)=0.6.
Newton gives 0-(-6)/2=3, the exact minimizer.
Newton uses more curvature information but requires computing and solving with the Hessian, which can be expensive or unstable in large nonconvex problems.
rubric: Gradient descent result 0.6.
Newton result 3.
Explains curvature and computational tradeoff.
theory.discussionPrompt: For f(w)=(w-3)², start at w=0. Compare one gradient descent step with learning rate 0.1 to one Newton minimization step. What practical tradeoff does Newton introduce?

theory.title: Optional: return versus risk
theory.prompt: Two equally weighted assets have standard deviations 10% and 20% and zero correlation. Give portfolio variance in decimal-return units and portfolio standard deviation.
theory.concepts: Portfolio return is a weighted sum, so variance includes weighted individual variances and cross-covariance terms. Diversification can reduce risk when assets are imperfectly correlated; expected return alone does not measure uncertainty. Correlation zero is not the same as independence. This optional finance track provides an application of covariance rather than a prerequisite for ML study.
hints: Use decimal standard deviations 0.1 and 0.2.
Var(aX+bY)=a²Var(X)+b²Var(Y)+2abCov(X,Y).
steps: Covariance is 0×0.1×0.2=0.
Standard deviation = sqrt(0.0125)≈0.1118, or 11.18%.
Positive correlation increases the covariance contribution; negative correlation decreases it. Weights and marginal volatilities also matter.
rubric: Variance 0.0125 in decimal-return units.
Standard deviation about 11.18%.
Explains the correlation contribution.
theory.discussionPrompt: Two assets have returns with standard deviations 10% and 20%, and correlation zero. A portfolio holds equal weights. Compute its return variance and standard deviation. Explain what correlation changes.

theory.title: Optional: a call option payoff
theory.prompt: A European call has strike 100 and premium 8. Ignoring interest and fees, give its payoff and buyer profit at expiration prices 90, 105, and 120. Distinguish a payoff from a price.
theory.concepts: A call gives the right, not the obligation, to buy an underlying asset at the strike. Its expiration payoff is max(S-K,0). Buyer profit subtracts the premium paid. The option’s pre-expiration price also reflects time, uncertainty, interest, and other contract assumptions; it is not generally equal to today’s immediate exercise payoff. European exercise occurs only at expiration.
hints: The right need not be exercised when S is below the strike.
Subtract the premium only for profit.
steps: At S=90, payoff=max(90-100,0)=0 and profit=-8.
At S=105, payoff=5 and profit=5-8=-3.
At S=120, payoff=20 and profit=20-8=12.
Expiration breakeven is S=108 under the stated simplifications. A positive payoff can still leave a loss after the premium.
rubric: Payoffs 0,5,20.
Profits -8,-3,12.
Distinguishes payoff, profit, and pre-expiration price.

theory.title: Optional: present value
theory.prompt: A certain payment of 110 arrives one year from now. The effective annual discount rate is 10%. What is its present value?
theory.concepts: Discounting converts future cash flows into equivalent current amounts under a specified rate convention. With annual effective rate r and t years, PV=FV/(1+r)^t. With a continuously compounded annual rate c, PV=FV exp(-ct). The same numeric rate under different compounding conventions represents a different accumulation factor. Risky cash flows require additional modeling and are outside this simple calculation.
hints: Invert the one-year growth factor 1.1.
Keep rate conventions distinct.
steps: One-year present value is 110/1.10=100.
If the same 110 arrives in two years at the same effective annual rate, PV=110/(1.1)²≈90.91.
For continuously compounded rate c, discount by exp(-ct).
An effective annual 10% rate corresponds to continuous rate log(1.1), not 0.10 exactly.
rubric: One-year PV 100.
Two-year formula and value about 90.91.
Correct continuous-compounding formula and convention distinction.
theory.discussionPrompt: A certain payment of 110 is due one year from now. With an effective annual discount rate of 10%, find its present value. How would two years and continuous compounding change the formula?

theory.title: Diagnose underfitting and overfitting
theory.prompt: Model A has high training and validation error. Model B has very low training error but high validation error. Diagnose each and propose useful next experiments. Why is a held-out test set still needed?
theory.concepts: Bias reflects systematic limitations in the fitted model, while variance describes sensitivity to the sampled training data. A model with too little flexibility can underfit; an overly flexible fit can chase training noise. Training and validation curves provide evidence, not a definitive diagnosis: distribution shift, bugs, or a poor metric can mimic these patterns. Validation supports model selection, while an untouched test set estimates performance after those choices.
hints: Compare the gap as well as the absolute error.
Repeated tuning can overfit the validation set.
steps: A’s high error on both splits suggests underfitting, insufficient features, or optimization failure. Check a baseline, training correctness, and then more capacity/features.
B’s large gap suggests overfitting. Try stronger regularization, early stopping, more data, or reduced capacity.
Check that splits represent deployment and that preprocessing is correct before drawing conclusions.
Keep the test set untouched until final evaluation because repeated validation-based decisions can overfit the validation data.
rubric: Recognizes underfitting and overfitting patterns.
Proposes appropriate experiments with caveats.
Explains untouched final testing.

theory.title: Find the leakage in a pipeline
theory.prompt: A colleague standardizes the full dataset, selects features using all labels, then runs cross-validation. Explain the problem and describe the correct procedure, including how to handle a future-time prediction task.
theory.concepts: Leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time or outside a training fold influences fitting. Validation then measures a procedure that had access to held-out information. Put learned transformations and feature selection inside the training process for each fold. Split design must match deployment: future prediction calls for chronological separation, and repeated people or devices may require grouped splits.
hints: Which steps learn statistics or use labels?
Every validation fold must stay unseen during fitting.
steps: Full-data scaling leaks held-out feature statistics; label-based selection leaks held-out targets even more directly.
For every fold, fit the scaler and selector only on that fold’s training rows.
Transform validation rows with those fitted objects, then score the model. Use a pipeline to enforce the sequence.
For future prediction, use time-respecting splits and ensure features were available at the prediction timestamp. Reserve a final future holdout.
rubric: Identifies both leaking operations.
Fits transformations within each training fold.
Addresses temporal availability and split design.

theory.title: Interpret a regression coefficient
theory.prompt: A fitted salary model is salary_in_thousands = 30 + 2×experience_years + 5×degree_indicator. Interpret the experience and degree coefficients. Does the model prove a degree causes a salary increase?
theory.concepts: Multiple linear regression describes the conditional mean as an additive combination of features. Each coefficient is interpreted holding the other modeled features fixed. Indicator variables compare a category with its reference category. Statistical association alone does not establish causality: omitted variables, selection, and confounding can explain a relationship. Extrapolating beyond observed experience or treating an implausible intercept as meaningful also requires caution.
hints: Specify units and what is held constant.
Prediction and causal inference require different assumptions.
steps: One additional experience year is associated with 2 thousand higher predicted salary, holding the degree indicator fixed.
Degree=1 is associated with 5 thousand higher predicted salary than degree=0 at the same experience.
The intercept predicts 30 thousand for experience zero and degree zero, if that situation is meaningful in the data.
The fitted association does not prove causation. A causal claim needs a suitable design and assumptions addressing confounding and selection.
rubric: Correct units and conditional interpretations.
Degree comparison uses reference group.
Rejects an unsupported causal conclusion.

theory.title: Logistic regression and odds
theory.prompt: A binary model has log-odds z=-2+0.5x. What is the probability at x=4, and by what factor do the odds change for a one-unit increase in x?
theory.concepts: Logistic regression models log(p/(1-p)) as a linear function of features. The sigmoid p=1/(1+exp(-z)) maps any real score into (0,1). A coefficient changes log-odds additively and odds multiplicatively, not probability by a fixed amount. A decision threshold converts the estimated class probability into a label. That threshold should reflect error costs and operational constraints.
hints: At x=4, the linear score is zero.
Exponentiate the coefficient for an odds ratio.
steps: Increasing x by one multiplies odds by exp(0.5)≈1.6487.
The target is a binary class and the output is its probability; a threshold gives a class label. “Regression” refers to fitting a quantitative log-odds relationship.
rubric: Probability 0.5.
Odds multiplier about 1.65.
Distinguishes odds, probability, and classification threshold.
theory.discussionPrompt: A binary model has log-odds z=-2+0.5x. Compute the probability when x=4 and the odds multiplier for a one-unit increase in x. Why is this a classification model despite “regression” in its name?

theory.title: Ridge versus lasso
theory.prompt: Compare ridge and lasso penalties. Why standardize features before using them, and why must the regularization strength be selected without the test set?
theory.concepts: Ridge adds λ sum β_j² to the fitting loss, continuously shrinking coefficients. Lasso adds λ sum |β_j| and can set coefficients exactly to zero, giving a form of feature selection. The penalty depends on feature units: a feature measured in large numeric units can use a small coefficient and receive less penalty for the same effect. The intercept is usually excluded. More regularization generally increases bias and may reduce variance.
hints: Compare a squared coefficient penalty with an absolute-value penalty.
Think about changing meters to millimeters.
steps: Ridge uses an L2-squared penalty; lasso uses an L1 penalty and can yield sparse coefficients.
Standardize using training statistics so penalties are comparable across feature scales.
Tune λ on validation data or within cross-validation, including all preprocessing in each fold.
Use the test set once for final evaluation. Choosing λ by test error would turn the test data into model-selection data and bias the reported performance.
rubric: Correct penalties and sparsity distinction.
Explains scaling using coefficient units.
Uses validation/CV rather than the test set for tuning.

theory.title: What cross-validation estimates
theory.prompt: Describe 5-fold cross-validation for selecting between three regularization strengths. Why should you refit afterward? What would nested cross-validation add?
theory.concepts: Cross-validation rotates held-out subsets to estimate how a training procedure generalizes. In each fold, the entire procedure—including learned preprocessing—must be fit without the validation portion. Averaging fold scores reduces dependence on a single arbitrary split, though folds are correlated because their training sets overlap. Using the same folds to choose hyperparameters and report the best score introduces selection optimism.
hints: Each candidate needs five separate fits.
The final model can use all available training data after selection.
steps: Partition training data into five appropriate folds, using stratification/grouping/time rules when needed.
For each λ, fit on four folds and score on the remaining fold, repeating five times.
Choose λ using the average validation score, then refit that full pipeline on all training data.
Nested CV uses outer held-out folds to evaluate the inner selection procedure. An untouched final test set is another way to assess the chosen procedure.
rubric: All candidates evaluated on held-out folds.
Refits the complete pipeline after selection.
Explains outer evaluation versus inner tuning.

theory.title: Accuracy can hide failure
theory.prompt: Out of 1,000 examples, 20 are positive. A model predicts every example negative. Compute accuracy, precision, and recall for the positive class, using zero for undefined precision. What should you examine instead of accuracy alone?
theory.concepts: Metrics answer different questions. Accuracy counts all correct labels. Positive-class precision asks how many predicted positives are true, while recall asks how many actual positives are detected. A model can score high accuracy by ignoring a rare class. Threshold choice trades false positives against false negatives; the right operating point depends on the application. Examine a confusion matrix and positive-class behavior rather than a single aggregate number.
hints: A zero-denominator convention is not evidence of good predictions.
steps: Precision=TP/(TP+FP)=0/0, reported as 0 by the stated convention.
Recall=TP/(TP+FN)=0/20=0.
Inspect precision-recall behavior, error costs, and a confusion matrix. This model never detects a positive, despite its high accuracy.
rubric: Accuracy 98%, precision 0 by convention, recall 0.
Recognizes the undefined precision denominator.
Discusses imbalance and suitable evaluation.

theory.title: Trees, forests, and boosting
theory.prompt: Explain how a decision tree predicts, why a very deep tree can overfit, and the different ways random forests and gradient boosting combine trees.
theory.concepts: A decision tree recursively partitions feature space with split rules. Leaves predict a class distribution or a numeric aggregate. Deep trees can isolate very small groups and fit noise. Random forests average many trees fitted on bootstrap samples, with random feature subsets encouraging diversity. Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially to improve the current ensemble objective. The two methods use different training and regularization mechanisms.
hints: Compare independent ensemble members with sequential error correction.
Small leaves are flexible but noisy.
steps: A tree routes an example through split conditions to a leaf prediction.
A deep tree can create nearly pure tiny leaves, reducing training error while increasing variance.
A random forest averages/votes across randomized, bootstrapped trees, reducing variance through imperfectly correlated errors.
Boosting adds trees sequentially to follow loss-reducing directions, often residuals for squared loss. Learning rate, depth, and number of rounds control flexibility.
rubric: Explains splits and leaves.
Relates depth to variance.
Correctly distinguishes forest averaging from sequential boosting.

theory.title: Nearest neighbors and feature scale
theory.prompt: Explain k-nearest-neighbor classification. What happens as k changes from 1 to a much larger value? Why can unscaled features and high dimensionality cause problems?
theory.concepts: KNN predicts from nearby training examples under a distance measure, usually by a vote for classification. Small k permits flexible boundaries and high sensitivity to individual examples. Larger k smooths the boundary, often increasing bias while reducing variance. Euclidean distance depends on numeric feature scale. In high dimensions, data become sparse and local neighborhoods may cease to be meaningfully local without sufficient data or structure.
hints: A feature with values in thousands can dominate one measured between zero and one.
A larger vote pool smooths local fluctuations.
steps: Compute distances to training examples, select k closest, and use their class vote or class proportions.
k=1 can fit training data closely and react to noise; increasing k usually smooths predictions.
Fit feature scaling on training data when units would otherwise distort distance.
High dimensionality makes neighborhoods sparse and can weaken distance-based similarity; feature selection, dimensionality reduction, or another model may help.
rubric: Correct neighbor-vote procedure.
Explains k and the bias-variance tradeoff.
Covers scaling and dimensionality.

theory.title: K-means and its limitations
theory.prompt: Describe one full iteration of k-means and its objective. Why can two runs differ? Explain why a cluster should not automatically be treated as a true class.
theory.concepts: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distance to cluster centroids. Alternating assignment and centroid updates never increases the objective when each step is solved correctly, but can converge to a local solution. Initialization and feature scaling matter. K-means favors compact Euclidean clusters and requires choosing k. Unsupervised groups describe structure in features; they do not establish semantic labels or causal categories.
hints: Alternate nearest-centroid assignments and cluster means.
A non-increasing objective need not reach the global minimum.
steps: Assign every point to its nearest centroid under squared Euclidean distance.
Replace each centroid by the mean of its assigned points, handling empty clusters explicitly.
Repeat until assignments or objective stabilize. Different initial centroids can reach different local minima; multiple restarts help.
Clusters optimize a geometric criterion. Validate their usefulness and stability; they are not automatically real-world classes.
rubric: Correct assignment and update steps.
States squared-distance objective and initialization dependence.
Avoids equating unsupervised clusters with true labels.

theory.title: Why a neural network needs nonlinearities
theory.prompt: Show why two affine layers without an activation collapse into one affine layer. What does a ReLU change? Mention one limitation of ReLU.
theory.concepts: An affine layer computes Wx+b. Composing affine maps produces another affine map, regardless of depth, so it cannot represent nonlinear boundaries by depth alone. ReLU applies max(0,z) elementwise, creating piecewise-linear regions and allowing a network to model nonlinear relationships. ReLU has a zero gradient on negative inputs; some units can become inactive. Activation choice interacts with initialization and optimization.
hints: Expand W₂(W₁x+b₁)+b₂.
Consider what happens to a negative pre-activation.
steps: Expand the composition to (W₂W₁)x+(W₂b₁+b₂).
Define effective weight W=W₂W₁ and bias b=W₂b₁+b₂: this is one affine map.
Inserting ReLU between the layers prevents that general collapse by changing the map depending on which inputs are positive.
ReLU’s negative branch has zero gradient, so a unit that remains negative on all training examples may stop learning.
rubric: Shows the algebraic collapse.
Explains the nonlinear effect of ReLU.
Names a valid ReLU limitation.

theory.title: A correct PyTorch training step
theory.prompt: Describe the order of operations for one PyTorch mini-batch training step. Why clear gradients? How does evaluation differ from training?
theory.concepts: Training uses an optimizer to update parameters from gradients of a batch loss. PyTorch accumulates gradients into parameter .grad fields when backward is called; clearing them is needed between independent steps unless intentional gradient accumulation is used. model.train() and model.eval() control layer behaviors such as dropout. A no_grad context disables gradient recording but does not itself switch the model to evaluation mode.
hints: Forward, loss, backward, update; include gradient clearing.
eval() and no_grad() have different jobs.
steps: Enter model.train() for training and clear gradients with optimizer.zero_grad(), commonly set_to_none=True.
Compute predictions with a forward pass and calculate a scalar batch loss.
Call loss.backward(), then optimizer.step(). Repeat for the next batch.
For validation, use model.eval() and a no_grad or inference_mode context, compute metrics, and do not update parameters. Clearing gradients prevents unintended summation across batches.
rubric: Correct zero-grad/forward/loss/backward/step sequence.
Explains gradient accumulation.
Distinguishes eval mode from gradient disabling.

theory.title: Batch normalization versus layer normalization
theory.prompt: For activations shaped (batch,features), compare which dimensions batch normalization and layer normalization use for statistics. Why is eval mode particularly important for batch normalization?
theory.concepts: For a simple 2D activation matrix, batch normalization estimates each feature’s statistics across examples. Layer normalization estimates each example’s statistics across its features. Both usually add learned scale and offset. Standard batch normalization keeps running estimates for evaluation; layer normalization uses each input’s own statistics in both modes. Small batches and distribution shifts can affect batch statistics. Convolutional batch-normalization axes include spatial dimensions as well.
hints: One method pools across rows and the other across columns.
Running averages matter at inference.
steps: For (B,F), batch norm computes F sets of statistics over the B examples.
Layer norm computes B sets of statistics over the F features, assuming all features are normalized.
In standard batch norm, training uses batch statistics and updates running estimates; eval uses stored estimates.
Layer norm does not depend on other examples in the batch. Be explicit about tensor layout and normalization axes.
rubric: Correct statistics axes for the specified shape.
Explains batch norm running estimates in eval.
Describes layer norm per-example behavior.

theory.title: Attention in plain language
theory.source: Attention Is All You Need §3.2 · Introductory supplement
theory.prompt: Explain the roles of queries, keys, and values in scaled dot-product attention. Give the formula, its output shape for Q(n,d), K(m,d), V(m,v), and the reason for scaling by sqrt(d).
theory.concepts: Attention computes a data-dependent weighted average of value vectors. Queries describe what each output position is looking for, keys provide matching features, and values provide the information to combine. Dot products produce similarity scores. Softmax across keys gives nonnegative weights summing to one for each query. Larger feature dimension can increase score variance, so scaling helps avoid overly saturated softmax. Position information and masks add structure in sequence models.
hints: QKᵀ produces one score per query-key pair.
Apply softmax across the m keys.
steps: Compute S=QKᵀ/sqrt(d), which has shape (n,m).
Compute A=softmax(S, axis=keys), normalizing each row.
Output=AV has shape (n,v), a weighted sum of values for each query.
For roughly independent unit-variance query/key components, dot-product variance grows with d; sqrt(d) scaling keeps score scale more controlled.
rubric: Correct formula and normalization axis.
Correct score and output shapes.
Explains queries/keys/values and scaling.

theory.title: Embeddings and token prediction
theory.prompt: What is a token embedding? Explain next-token prediction and why a causal attention mask is necessary during training. Distinguish training from text generation.
theory.concepts: An embedding table maps discrete token IDs to learned dense vectors. A language model predicts a distribution over the vocabulary for the next token, using preceding tokens as context. Training can evaluate many positions in parallel using shifted targets, but each position must not see the token it is meant to predict. A causal mask blocks attention to future positions. During autoregressive generation, newly chosen tokens are appended one at a time.
hints: An embedding is a learned lookup, not an ordinal numeric interpretation of IDs.
Training targets are shifted one position relative to inputs.
steps: Look up a vector for each token ID from a vocabulary-by-dimension embedding matrix.
At position t, compute logits for token t+1 and minimize cross-entropy against the true next token.
Mask attention to future positions so target information cannot leak into the prediction.
Training uses known sequences and many parallel target positions; generation repeatedly chooses a next token and feeds the extended sequence back into the model.
rubric: Defines learned token lookup.
Explains shifted next-token objective.
Explains masking and autoregressive generation.

theory.title: Design a small prediction system
theory.prompt: You need to predict whether a customer will cancel within 30 days. Outline a first useful ML experiment: target definition, features, splitting, baseline, metrics, and monitoring. Identify one likely leakage trap.
theory.concepts: A useful ML system starts with an explicit prediction timestamp, target horizon, and action. Features must be available at that timestamp. Historical data should mimic deployment, including delays in observing labels and repeated users. A simple baseline and an evaluation metric tied to costs make improvements interpretable. Monitoring checks input quality, performance after labels arrive, and changes in the population; deployment alone does not guarantee sustained accuracy.
hints: Start with what is known when a prediction is made.
Choose a split that reflects future use and repeated customers.
steps: Define one row per customer at a specified timestamp and label cancellation in the next 30 days; allow the label window to mature.
Use only historical information available at that timestamp. Future cancellation reason or refund events would leak the target.
Use a time-aware split, with group handling appropriate to whether deployment predicts existing or new customers; fit preprocessing only on training data.
Compare a base-rate predictor and logistic regression. Evaluate recall/precision at a workable intervention budget, plus calibration if probabilities drive decisions.
Monitor missingness and feature distributions immediately, and outcome-based metrics once labels mature. Check performance by relevant cohorts and retrain based on evidence.
rubric: Clear target, timestamp, and horizon.
Leak-free features and realistic split.
Baseline, practical metrics, and monitoring.

readings.title: From prediction task to trustworthy evaluation

sections.title: 1. Define what is being predicted
sections.body: Supervised learning uses examples with features X and a target y to learn a prediction rule. Regression predicts a numerical quantity; classification predicts a category or its probability. Start with a prediction timestamp and target horizon: “Will this customer cancel in the next 30 days?” is more precise than “Predict churn.” Every input must be available at that timestamp. A future refund or cancellation reason would reveal information about the answer.

sections.title: 2. Separate fitting from evaluation
sections.body: Training data fit model parameters. Validation data choose hyperparameters, thresholds, and other design decisions. A final untouched test set estimates the performance of the selected procedure. Preprocessing is part of fitting: means, imputations, feature selection, and learned encodings belong inside each training fold. A pipeline prevents accidentally using held-out information. For future predictions, use time-respecting splits; for repeated entities, decide whether groups must be held apart.

sections.title: 3. Diagnose the gap
sections.body: High training and validation errors can indicate underfitting, weak features, or optimization failure. Low training error with high validation error suggests overfitting, but also check distribution differences and bugs. More capacity can reduce underfitting; regularization, more data, and early stopping can reduce overfitting. Compare with a simple baseline before investing in complexity.

sections.title: Worked example: a misleading score
sections.body: Suppose only 20 of 1,000 customers cancel. A model that always predicts “no cancellation” has 980/1,000=98% accuracy but zero recall for cancellations. If the action is a limited retention campaign, evaluate precision and recall at the number of customers you can actually contact. Keep probability calibration in mind when decisions depend on estimated risks.

sections.title: Before you practice
sections.body: Be able to explain why fitting a scaler on the full dataset leaks information, why validation is not a permanently untouched test set, and why deployment conditions determine the split. Write down a baseline, a metric, and a plausible source of leakage for your own example.

readings.title: Linear regression, logistic regression, and regularization

sections.title: 1. Linear prediction and squared error
sections.body: Linear regression predicts y_hat = Xw+b. Each coefficient describes a conditional association while holding the other modeled features fixed. Least squares minimizes squared residuals. The gradient of mean((Xw-y)²) is (2/n)Xᵀ(Xw-y) when no intercept is included. The normal equations describe an optimum, but in code use a stable least-squares solver rather than explicitly inverting XᵀX. Correlated columns can make coefficients unstable even if predictions remain similar.

sections.title: 2. Probabilities and log-odds
sections.body: Logistic regression instead models z=wᵀx+b and p=1/(1+exp(-z)). The linear score is a log-odds, log(p/(1-p)). Increasing feature j by one changes odds by a factor exp(w_j), not probability by a fixed amount. A probability is not yet an action: a threshold turns it into a label. Choose that threshold using error costs or operational constraints, using validation data.

sections.title: 3. Control flexibility
sections.body: Ridge adds a squared L2 coefficient penalty and shrinks coefficients smoothly. Lasso adds an L1 penalty and can set coefficients to zero. Standardize features using training statistics so that the penalty does not arbitrarily favor one measurement unit. Usually the intercept is not penalized. Select penalty strength using validation or cross-validation, then refit the complete procedure on all training data.

sections.title: Worked example: odds are not probabilities
sections.body: With z=-2+0.5x, x=4 gives z=0 and p=1/2. Moving to x=5 gives z=0.5, odds exp(0.5)≈1.6487, and p≈0.6225. The coefficient multiplies the odds by about 1.65; it does not add 0.5 to the probability.

sections.title: Before you practice
sections.body: Check matrix shapes before differentiating. Explain the difference between a fitted association and a causal effect. Be able to say why coefficient penalties depend on feature scale, and why you must not tune the penalty on the test set.

sections.title: 1. Learn from nearby examples
sections.body: K-nearest neighbors predicts using the training examples closest to the new input. For classification it usually takes a vote; for regression it averages targets. Small k permits a flexible boundary and is sensitive to noise. Large k smooths the result, usually increasing bias and reducing variance. Distance depends on units, so scale features when appropriate. In high dimensions, sparse neighborhoods and irrelevant features can weaken similarity.

sections.title: 2. Partition the feature space
sections.body: A decision tree asks a sequence of feature-threshold questions. Each split partitions the examples; a leaf stores a class distribution or a numeric prediction. Deep trees can isolate tiny groups and fit noise. Limit depth, require larger leaves, or prune using validation. Unlike distance-based models, ordinary axis-aligned trees generally do not need standardization just to accommodate different numeric units.

sections.title: 3. Combine imperfect models
sections.body: A random forest averages randomized trees trained with bootstrap samples and random feature subsets. Its main benefit is reducing variance when tree errors are not perfectly correlated. Gradient boosting builds an ensemble sequentially: each new tree improves the current loss, following residuals for squared-error regression. Boosting learning rate, tree depth, and number of rounds all affect flexibility. Neither approach removes the need for leak-free evaluation.

sections.title: Worked comparison
sections.body: A deep single tree memorizes training data but changes sharply when a few examples change. Averaging many diverse trees can stabilize it. Boosting takes a different route: it builds a strong predictor through many incremental corrections. A forest is not simply boosting with a different name.

sections.title: Before you practice
sections.body: Explain one prediction from each model in plain language. Distinguish a model’s training cost from its prediction cost, and compare how scaling and depth or neighborhood size affect it.

sections.title: 1. PCA finds variance directions
sections.body: Center features before ordinary PCA. The covariance matrix describes spread and linear co-movement. Its eigenvectors give orthogonal principal directions; its eigenvalues give the variance along them. The first principal component maximizes projected variance, and later components maximize remaining variance subject to orthogonality. Choosing a sign for a component is arbitrary. Scaling features changes the result, so decide whether units or standardized variation should matter.

sections.title: 2. Explained variance is not predictive value
sections.body: For covariance diag(4,1), the first coordinate explains 4/(4+1)=80% of variance. That does not guarantee it is useful for predicting a target. PCA is unsupervised: a low-variance direction could contain the most important label information. If PCA is part of a predictive pipeline, fit it on training data only and select the number of components without the final test set.

sections.title: 3. K-means groups by distance
sections.body: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distance to cluster means. Alternate assigning points to their nearest centroid and replacing each centroid with its cluster’s mean. Initialization can lead to different local optima; multiple restarts help. Feature scaling matters, and k must be selected. Empty clusters require explicit handling. A cluster is a geometric grouping, not automatically a real-world category.

sections.title: Before you practice
sections.body: Be able to distinguish dimensionality reduction from clustering. Explain why the highest-variance direction need not be the most predictive, and why a stable cluster assignment still needs domain validation.

readings.title: Neural networks and the training loop

sections.title: 1. Affine layers need nonlinearities
sections.body: An affine layer forms Wx+b. Two affine layers without an activation collapse into one: W₂(W₁x+b₁)+b₂=(W₂W₁)x+(W₂b₁+b₂). ReLU, max(0,z), changes which linear relationship applies in different input regions. This permits nonlinear mappings. Its negative branch has zero gradient, so units that remain negative can stop receiving useful updates.

sections.title: 2. Match the loss to the task
sections.body: Squared error suits many numeric targets. For multiclass classification, the model outputs one raw logit per class. Cross-entropy measures the negative log-probability assigned to the correct class. PyTorch cross_entropy expects raw logits and integer class indices, and combines a stable log-softmax with the loss. Do not feed it softmax probabilities as though they were logits. A batch mean loss is a scalar suitable for backpropagation.

sections.title: 3. One complete update
sections.body: Set training mode, clear gradients, run the forward pass, calculate the loss, call backward, then update parameters with the optimizer. PyTorch accumulates gradients, so clearing them avoids unintended accumulation across independent batches. Autograd follows the chain rule through the computation graph; it does not choose an optimizer or clear gradients for you. Track both training and validation loss to catch divergence or overfitting.

sections.title: 4. Evaluation is a separate mode
sections.body: Use model.eval() to change behaviors such as dropout and standard batch normalization. Use no_grad() or inference_mode() to avoid recording a gradient graph when it is not needed. These operations have different purposes: no_grad alone does not disable dropout. Do not update model parameters on validation data.

sections.title: Before you practice
sections.body: Trace tensor shapes from a batch through a linear layer to logits and a scalar loss. Explain why an activation is needed, why gradients are cleared, and why eval mode is different from disabling gradient recording.

readings.title: Normalization, embeddings, and attention
readings.source: ISLP chapter 10; Attention Is All You Need §3.2 · Original review lesson

sections.title: 1. Normalize over the intended axes
sections.body: For a matrix (batch,features), batch normalization computes feature statistics across examples and typically keeps running statistics for inference. Layer normalization computes statistics across features within each example. A basic layer norm is (x-mean)/sqrt(variance+epsilon), often followed by learned scale and bias. Use population variance for the standard layer-normalization formula. Epsilon goes inside the square root.

sections.title: 2. Turn tokens into vectors
sections.body: A token embedding is a learned lookup table from token IDs to dense vectors. IDs identify entries; the distance between integer IDs is not semantic similarity. A next-token model predicts a vocabulary distribution from preceding tokens. During training, targets are shifted relative to inputs. Causal masking prevents a position from seeing future target information, even when many training positions are processed in parallel.

sections.title: 3. Attention is a weighted combination
sections.body: Queries describe what an output position is looking for. Keys provide matching features; values provide information to combine. With Q(n,d), K(m,d), and V(m,v), compute scores QKᵀ/sqrt(d), normalize each row across its m keys with softmax, then multiply by V. Scores and weights have shape (n,m); the output has shape (n,v). Each output is a weighted sum of value vectors.

sections.title: Worked example and scale
sections.body: If one query gives equal scores to two keys, softmax assigns weights 1/2 and 1/2. Values [2,4] and [4,8] therefore combine to [3,6]. Under roughly independent unit-variance components, a d-dimensional dot product has variance proportional to d; division by sqrt(d) controls score scale and helps avoid saturating softmax. Numerically stable softmax also subtracts each row maximum before exponentiation.

coding.prompt: Given nonempty strings containing only 0 and 1, return their binary sum as a string. Return canonical output with no leading zeros except "0". Implement digit addition without converting entire strings to integers. Inputs are valid as specified. Do not mutate input arrays/lists.
coding.concepts: Positional addition works from the least significant digit toward the most significant one. Each position contributes its two input bits and a carry. The output bit is total modulo 2 and the next carry is total divided by 2. This is O(n+m) time and O(max(n,m)) output storage.

def add_binary(a, b):
    i, j, carry = len(a)-1, len(b)-1, 0
    out = []
    while i >= 0 or j >= 0 or carry:
        total = carry
        if i >= 0: total += int(a[i]); i -= 1
        if j >= 0: total += int(b[j]); j -= 1
        out.append(str(total % 2))
        carry = total // 2
    return "".join(reversed(out)).lstrip("0") or "0"

        if i >= window: total -= values[i-window]
        out.append(total/min(window,i+1))
    return out

import numpy as np
def sigmoid(x):
    out = np.empty_like(x,dtype=float)
    positive = x >= 0
    out[positive] = 1/(1+np.exp(-x[positive]))
    exp_x = np.exp(x[~positive])
    out[~positive] = exp_x/(1+exp_x)
    return out

def cosine_matrix(a, b):
    an = np.linalg.norm(a,axis=1,keepdims=True)

coding.prompt: For finite nonempty routing logits (T,E), return alpha*E*dot(f,P) as a Python float, default alpha=0.01. f is each expert’s fraction of top-1 assignments (ties choose lowest index). P is each expert’s mean stable-softmax probability over ALL tokens. Do not round. Inputs are valid as specified. Do not mutate input arrays/lists.
coding.concepts: A sparse expert router has a hard workload summary and a soft preference summary. Their dot product forms an auxiliary objective that can backpropagate through the probability mean while treating hard assignments as fixed. coding.solution:
import numpy as np
def balance_loss(logits, alpha=0.01):
    e = np.exp(logits-logits.max(axis=1,keepdims=True))
    p = e/e.sum(axis=1,keepdims=True)
    t, experts = logits.shape
    fractions = np.bincount(logits.argmax(axis=1),minlength=experts)/t
    return float(alpha*experts*np.dot(fractions,p.mean(axis=0)))

import numpy as np
def topk_routes(logits, k):
    chosen = np.argsort(-logits,axis=1,kind="stable")[:,:k]
    scores = np.take_along_axis(logits,chosen,axis=1)
    e = np.exp(scores-scores.max(axis=1,keepdims=True))
    out = np.zeros_like(logits,dtype=float)
    np.put_along_axis(out,chosen,e/e.sum(axis=1,keepdims=True),axis=1)
    return out

coding.prompt: For Q and K of shape (T,D) and V (T,H), return softmax((Q@K.T)/sqrt(D) with future positions masked,dim=-1)@V. A token may attend to itself and earlier tokens only. No dropout; return shape (T,H). Inputs are valid as specified. Do not mutate input arrays/lists.

import torch
def causal_attention(q, k, v):
    scores = q@k.T/(q.shape[-1]**0.5)
    future = torch.triu(torch.ones_like(scores,dtype=torch.bool),diagonal=1)
    return torch.softmax(scores.masked_fill(future,float("-inf")),dim=-1)@v

sql.concepts: WHERE filters individual rows before they appear in the output. Comparisons such as >= and = produce conditions; AND requires both conditions to hold. A text literal such as paid is written as 'paid'. The operator >= includes the boundary, unlike >. A query can use a column to filter without returning that column.

guide.title: Build two tests
guide.body: First check the order status, then the amount. Join the conditions with AND so an expensive pending order is excluded.

guide.title: Work the example
guide.body: Order 101 is paid but only 40, so exclude it. Orders 102 and 104 are paid and at least 50, so include them. The boundary fixture also includes an amount of exactly 50.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: Do not quote column names as string literals. status = 'paid' compares a column with text; 'status' = 'paid' compares two constant strings.

hints: Use WHERE status = 'paid'.
Add AND amount >= 50.
steps: Read orders.
Keep paid rows with amount >= 50.
Return id and amount.

sql.title: 03 · Find missing values
sql.prompt: Return id and name for customers whose city is missing. Output columns: id, name. Any row order.

Ordinary comparisons involving NULL evaluate to unknown, which WHERE does not keep. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL for explicit missing-value tests. A result with no rows is a valid result, not a query failure.

guide.title: Missing is not text
guide.body: Use IS NULL rather than a comparison to the word 'NULL'. That quoted word is an ordinary text value.

guide.title: Work the example
guide.body: Cleo’s city is missing in the practice shop, so return Cleo’s id and name. In some alternate shops there can be no missing cities.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: city = NULL does not find missing entries. The database’s three-valued logic treats that equality as unknown.

hints: The predicate is city IS NULL.
Return the requested identity columns, not the city column.
steps: Read customers.
Filter city with IS NULL.
Select id and name.

sql.title: 04 · Sort and take the first rows
sql.prompt: Return the two most expensive paid orders, or fewer if fewer exist. Sort amount descending, then id ascending to break ties. Output columns: id, amount. Order is checked.
sql.concepts: ORDER BY determines result order. DESC means largest first; ASC means smallest first and is the default. Multiple sort keys are applied left to right. LIMIT restricts how many sorted rows are returned. Without an explicit tie-breaker, selecting the top rows among equal amounts can be nondeterministic.

guide.title: Query order
guide.body: Write SELECT … FROM … WHERE … ORDER BY … LIMIT … . Filtering happens before ranking, so pending orders never compete for the top two.

guide.title: Work the example
guide.body: Paid amounts are 40, 75, and 60, so return order 102 before 104. If two amounts tie, the smaller id comes first.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: LIMIT 2 alone does not mean the two greatest values. Sort first, and do not include pending orders.

hints: Filter paid orders before sorting.
Use ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC followed by LIMIT 2.
steps: Keep only paid orders.
Sort amount descending and id ascending.
Limit the result to two rows.
sql.solution:
SELECT id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 2;

sql.title: 05 · Count orders for each customer
sql.prompt: For every customer_id that appears in orders, return customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, and SUM(amount) AS total_amount. Include all statuses and allow the NULL customer_id group. Any row order.
sql.concepts: An aggregate combines several input rows into a summary. GROUP BY creates one group per distinct grouping key. COUNT(*) counts rows, while SUM adds non-NULL values. AS names an output expression. Every selected non-aggregate expression here is a grouping key. A customer with no orders has no group in this query.

guide.title: From rows to groups
guide.body: Imagine sorting order rows into buckets by customer_id. Count the rows in each bucket and add their amounts.

guide.title: Work the example
guide.body: Customer 1 has two orders totaling 115. Customer 2 has one order totaling 20. All statuses count because no WHERE filter was requested.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: COUNT(customer_id) skips NULL values; COUNT(*) still counts a row whose customer_id is NULL. Do not group by the unique order id.

hints: Use GROUP BY customer_id.
Alias COUNT(*) as order_count and SUM(amount) as total_amount.
steps: Group orders by customer_id.
Count all rows and sum their amounts.
Apply the requested aliases.

sql.title: 06 · Filter grouped results
sql.prompt: Return customer_id and SUM(amount) AS paid_total for customers whose paid orders sum to at least 100. Exclude NULL customer_id. Any row order.
sql.concepts: WHERE filters source rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Use WHERE to keep paid orders with a known customer, then GROUP BY to summarize those rows, then HAVING to keep large totals. SUM(amount) in a WHERE clause would be at the wrong stage for this question.

guide.title: Separate two decisions
guide.body: A paid order is a row-level condition. A total of at least 100 is a group-level condition. Put the two filters in different clauses.

guide.title: Work the example
guide.body: In the practice shop, customer 1 has paid orders of 40 and 75, totaling 115, so qualifies. Customer 3 has only 60 and does not qualify.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: Do not filter individual amounts to >=100: several smaller orders may add to a qualifying total. Use the inclusive boundary in HAVING.

hints: First use WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL.
After grouping, use HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100.
steps: Filter paid rows with a nonmissing customer_id.
Group by customer_id and sum amounts.
Keep groups whose sum is >=100.
sql.solution:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100;

sql.title: 07 · Match rows across two tables
sql.prompt: For every paid order that matches a customer, return orders.id AS order_id, customers.name AS customer_name, and orders.amount. Any row order.
sql.concepts: A join relates rows from tables using a matching condition. Here orders.customer_id refers to customers.id. INNER JOIN keeps matching pairs only. Short aliases such as o and c make shared column names unambiguous. One customer can match multiple orders, so a join can produce several rows for the same customer name.

guide.title: State the relationship
guide.body: Join on customer identity: o.customer_id = c.id. Do not join on order id or on a name that may be repeated.

guide.title: Work the example
guide.body: Ada matches both of her paid orders, so her name appears twice. A paid order with a NULL customer_id has no matching customer and is omitted by an inner join.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: An omitted ON condition creates unrelated row combinations. DISTINCT would hide repeated names but would also change the requested one-row-per-order result.

hints: Use orders AS o JOIN customers AS c.
Match o.customer_id to c.id, then filter o.status.
steps: Join orders to customers using their key relationship.
Keep paid orders.
Select and alias the requested three columns.
sql.solution:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer_name, o.amount
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';

sql.title: 08 · Find customers with no orders
sql.prompt: Return id and name for customers who have no orders of ANY status. Any row order. Use a LEFT JOIN in your practice attempt.

A customer with a pending order still has an order and must be excluded.

guide.title: Preserve customers
guide.body: Start from customers and LEFT JOIN orders on customer identity. This keeps customers whose match is absent.

guide.title: Detect the missing match
guide.body: Filter the joined result with o.id IS NULL. Selecting c.id rather than o.id returns the customer identity you want.

guide.title: Common mistake
guide.body: An inner join discards the unmatched customers too early. Filtering paid orders would instead answer “no paid orders,” which is a different task.

hints: Keep customers on the left side of LEFT JOIN.
After joining, use WHERE o.id IS NULL.
steps: Left-join all orders onto customers.
Keep rows where the order-side id is NULL.
Return customer id and name.
sql.solution:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
